Two of the most famous synthesizers ever made are close relatives. The **Minimoog Model D** (Moog, 1970) put a modular synth's
oscillators, filter and envelopes behind fixed switches in a box you could take on stage. The **Prophet-5** (Sequential
Circuits, 1978) did almost the same thing five times over, one voice per note, and added a microprocessor that remembered
every knob. On this page each is rebuilt in the browser. You can turn a sound on one into the nearest sound on the other and
read what happened to every setting: **the same**, **close** or **impossible**, and why.

Both panels here are drawn after the real ones and are not copies; the names belong to their makers. Every fact about the
real instruments comes from their manuals and is cited with its page. Anything the manuals do not say, such as how a
Prophet knob numbered 0 to 10 maps to hertz, is this page's own choice and is marked so.

## The two synths

<div class="scmp"></div>

**How to use it.** Pick an **Example**, then press **▶ Model D**, **▶ Prophet-5** or **▶ One, then the other**. Turn any
knob on the top panel and the bottom one follows. **Turn into the …** makes the other synth the starting point. Point at a
line of the report to light up the controls it is about on both panels. Coloured outlines on the panels show
<span class="scmp-tag scmp-exact">the same</span>, <span class="scmp-tag scmp-approx">close</span> and
<span class="scmp-tag scmp-lost">cannot be done</span>.

The **From** and **To** pickers choose any two of the seventeen synths. A **What if…** menu on some panels adds a feature the real
instrument lacks (see [What if…](#what-if)); the panel is then outlined and badged, and the report still describes the real one.

## The Model D patch sheets

The Model D manual ends with patch sheets: a drawing of the front panel for each sound, with orange pointers on the knobs,
light-blue circles round the chosen range and wave, and the switches coloured on the side that is pressed (Moog Music,
*Minimoog Model D* manual, pp. 55–76; blank sheets to copy on pp. 77–79). Below, each one is redrawn in the same layout.
Pick a sheet, turn the knobs on it, press **▶ Play** to hear it on the Model D panel above, or **Show on the panel above** to
compare it knob by knob. **One part at a time** shows a single section with **Back** and **Next**; **Large print** and
**High contrast** make it easier to read. The readings were taken from the printed pages to the nearest half mark; the ones
that were hard to read are listed under the sheet. Times on the contour knobs follow the printed scale (10 ms to 10 s); how
the cutoff knob maps to hertz is this page's choice, as on the panel above.

<div class="moog-sheets"></div>

## The Prophet-5 guide's patches

The Prophet-5 Rev4 User's Guide prints no patch charts or factory list (its factory programs live only in the instrument). It does print recipes that start from the Basic Program and set knobs to numbers. Ten of them are in the **Example** menu at the top as "Guide p. …": the Basic Program, the filter and envelope tutorials, the synth bass (short, long and fatter), synth brass, the string pad and the hard-sync lead. Each says how well this panel follows it: *exact* where the guide prints a number this panel takes, *approx* where the guide only says "turn up" or "slightly" and the value is this page's guess (unverified). Controls the guide does not name keep the Basic Program, most of which the guide does not print.

## What they share

Both are **subtractive synths** ([Sound 7](sound-subtractive.qmd)). Oscillators make a wave full of harmonics, a mixer
blends them, and a **4-pole, 24 dB-per-octave low-pass filter** takes harmonics away. One envelope moves the filter and
another moves the loudness. On both, resonance can be turned up until the filter whistles by itself. So a plain bass or
lead translates almost knob for knob: try **Fat bass** and look at how few red lines there are. The filter plot shows two
curves with the same slope. The difference is in how they *sound* when pushed, because the filters are different
circuits: the Moog **ladder**, and on the Prophet-5 either Dave Rossum's SSI 2140 (the sound of the first Prophets, "Rev
1/2") or Doug Curtis's CEM 3320 ("Rev 3"). Flip the Prophet's **Rev** switch and listen.

## What only the Model D can do

- **Three oscillators on every note.** A Prophet voice has two. The **Lead in fifths and fourths** example (from the Model D
  manual) tunes oscillator 2 a fifth up and oscillator 3 a fourth down, so each key plays a three-note chord. On the
  Prophet-5 the third pitch is gone. Its **Chord memory** can hold such a stack, but only by playing it with several voices.
- **Feeding its own output back in.** With nothing plugged into its external input, the Model D's output runs back into
  its mixer. Turn that input up and the mixer **overloads**, which makes a growling, compressed sound. Watch the
  **Mixer drive** plot bend over in **Overdriven bass**. The Prophet's mixer can also be driven hard, but it has no path
  from its output back to its input.
- **A spare oscillator as the modulator.** Oscillator 3 can leave the keyboard and run as a slow LFO, or at audio speed
  for FM, while oscillators 1 and 2 sound. On the Prophet the only oscillator that can modulate is B, so once B is busy
  sounding there is nothing left.

## What only the Prophet-5 can do

- **Chords.** Five voices, so five notes at once. Play **String pad** on both and the Model D keeps only the lowest
  note, which is how a classic Model D chooses.
- **Hard sync.** Oscillator A restarts every time oscillator B does. Sweeping A's pitch with the filter envelope through
  Poly Mod gives the famous tearing lead (**Hard-sync lead**, from the Prophet's guide). The Model D has no sync.
- **Moving pulse width.** The Prophet's pulse width is a knob that the LFO or Poly Mod can sweep, which gives the
  chorused, shimmering tone of **Pulse-width-modulated strings**. The Model D's pulse widths are fixed positions of a
  switch.
- **Poly Mod.** Every voice's filter envelope or oscillator B can modulate its own oscillator A or filter. That is
  sync sweeps and FM *in chords*. The Model D can do FM (**Oscillator 3 frequency-modulating oscillator 1**), but for one
  note, with the depth on the mod wheel.
- **Memory.** The Prophet stores its sounds as programs (the original held 40). A Model D sound exists only while the
  knobs stay where they are.

## What only the TB-303 can do

- **Accent and slide on each step.** The TB-303's sequencer stores pitch, length, accent and slide for every step (TB-303
  manual p. 89). An accented step is louder and brighter by as much as the ACCENT knob says (p. 34). A slide step glides into
  the next one. Try **Acid line** and translate it: no other synth here has accent, so it becomes velocity at best.
- **Almost nothing else.** One oscillator with two waveforms and five tone knobs (p. 34). The lesson goes the other way:
  most patches from the other synths lose a great deal on the 303. Its filter is a 24 dB low-pass that does not whistle on
  its own (Wikipedia; unverified).

## What only the Juno-60 can do

- **The chorus.** Chorus I, or the stronger II, is built in (Juno-60 manual p. 22). Every other synth here loses it in
  **PWM strings with chorus II**.
- **A sub-oscillator and a high-pass filter** next to one DCO (pp. 13-14). The Juno-106's HPF at 0 boosts the bass instead
  (Juno-106 manual p. 18), and the 106 adds portamento, which the Juno-60's DCO does not have (Juno-60 p. 12; Juno-106 p. 23):
  flip **Model** to 106.
- **One envelope for everything.** Filter and loudness share one ADSR (p. 16), so patches from synths with two envelopes
  lose one of them.

## What only the ARP 2600 can do

- **Patch cords on top of the normals.** Every input of the 2600 already has a connection inside, which a cord replaces
  (2600 M manual pp. 5-15). VCO-2's sine reaches VCO-1, VCO-3 and the filter; sample-and-hold reaches every VCO. **Patch
  cords** on the panel add routes the other synths have no names for.
- **A ring modulator, sample-and-hold and three VCOs that can each be an LFO** (pp. 6-9, 15). Try **Ring-modulator bells**
  and **Sample-and-hold bleeps**.
- **Two envelopes of different kinds:** an ADSR and an AR, the VCA taking one linearly and the other exponentially (p. 12).

## What only the OB-Xa can do

- **A 2-pole filter as well as a 4-pole one.** The 4-POLE switch chooses 24 dB per octave (fuller), or 12 dB (brighter)
  when it is off (OB-Xa manual p. 11). Translate **2-pole brass pad** and compare the slopes on the filter plot.
- **Filter envelope on oscillator 2,** up to an octave, with sync (p. 10): **Sync lead**.
- **The SEM's filter modes.** The SEM's filter could be low-pass, band-pass, high-pass or notch (Wikipedia; unverified).
  The extra **SEM mode** switch is not on the OB-Xa. A band-pass patch is lost on every low-pass-only synth.

## What only the MS-20 can do

- **A resonant high-pass and low-pass filter in series**, each able to oscillate (MS-20 manual p. 5): **Screaming HP + LP**.
  Only the Juno also has a high-pass filter, and its filter has no resonance.
- **A patch panel, EG 1 with a delay, and EG 2 with a hold time** (pp. 6-7). Nothing else here delays a pitch sweep or holds a
  note after the key lifts.

## What only the DX7 can do

- **FM.** Six sine-wave operators, each with its own envelope of four rates and four levels, wired into one of 32 algorithms
  (DX7 manual pp. 23-26). The manual's first exercise sounds like "a saw-tooth wave which is going through a filter that has a
  lot of resonance" with "no filters involved" (p. 35). That one translates. **Bell** and **Electric-piano-like tine** do not:
  on every other synth the FM note in the report is red, and only an oscillator per carrier is left. This is the point of the
  comparison.
- **Sixteen voices** (PDF p. 4). Going the other way, the DX7 loses every filter, resonance and pulse-width setting, because
  there is nothing to set.

## What only the PPG Wave can do

- **Wavetables.** Each oscillator steps through a table of 64 waves, and an envelope or the LFO can move it (Sound On Sound's
  Wave 2.3 review): **Wavetable sweep by envelope**. Other synths keep one fixed wave. The page's four tables are its own,
  not the PPG's.
- Into **analog 24 dB filters** (SSM 2044, PPG Wave 2.3 service manual p. 5; Wikipedia). No owner's manual was found, so the
  panel layout is this page's (unverified).

## What only the Prophet-6 can do

- **Two digital effects in series, inside the instrument.** Effect A is a bucket-brigade or digital delay, a chorus or one of
  two phasers; Effect B can also be a hall, room, plate or spring reverb, because "reverb effects are only available as Effect
  B, since it's the last stage" (Prophet-6 manual pp. 26–27). Try **PWM pad through chorus and hall** and translate it: the
  effects are lost on everything but the Grandmother, which keeps only its spring. The effect sounds on this page are its own
  simple designs, not Sequential's.
- **Oscillator shapes between the waves.** Each shape knob moves smoothly from triangle to sawtooth to pulse, with
  "in-between" waves on the way (p. 15), and Poly Mod can move oscillator 1's shape (p. 34).
- **A resonant 2-pole high-pass as well as the 4-pole low-pass,** sharing one filter envelope, each with its own bipolar
  amount (pp. 20–22), and **Slop**, a control for how far out of tune the voices drift (p. 18).

## The Moog family

Five more Moogs sit in the pickers. They share this page's one ladder-filter model, so **the filter differences between them are
not measured and not modelled**: what differs is the panel, the routing and the envelopes, each from its own manual.

- **Taurus** (bass pedals): two sawtooth oscillators with BEAT to detune one, a 24 dB filter "flat to oscillation", a filter
  contour of attack and decay, a loudness attack, sustain and DECAY switch, and glide (Taurus 205A manual PDF pp. 3–6). Only the
  VARIABLE preset is on the panel; the three fixed presets' settings are not printed.
- **Voyager:** three oscillators whose waves turn smoothly from triangle to narrow pulse, sync and linear FM, and two filters:
  **Dual LP** (two low-passes side by side) or **HP/LP** (in series, a band-pass), with **Spacing** between them (Voyager Old
  School manual PDF p. 8). Here the second filter is a 2-pole, this page's simplification.
- **Sub 37:** **Duo mode** plays two notes at once, one on each oscillator, through the one filter; **MultiDrive** overdrives the
  filter stage; a square sub-oscillator sits an octave under oscillator 1. These are cited from the **Subsequent 25** manual, the
  same family, because the Sub 37 manual could not be obtained. On this page each Duo note gets its own filter copy, so the
  shared-filter sound is not modelled (unverified approximation). The sequencer and arpeggiator are left out.
- **Grandmother:** semi-modular, with a 1-pole high-pass utility that a cord can put before the filter, one ADSR, VCA modes ENV,
  KB RLS and DRONE, a real spring reverb tank and an LFO whose amounts come in through the mod wheel (Grandmother manual PDF
  pp. 7, 15–23). The spring here is a digital stand-in.
- **Memorymoog:** six voices of three oscillators each, waves that can be combined, Voice Modulation from the filter contour or
  oscillator 3, 100 programs (Memorymoog manual PDF pp. 5, 14–17). Its mixer clips past 4 or 5 (p. 17); here every mixer shares
  one soft curve.

## Two free software synths: Vital and Surge XT

Two of the seventeen are not hardware: **Vital** and **Surge XT** are free software synths that run as plug-ins in a DAW. Here each
is a **beginner panel**: a few of the real plug-in's controls, with its own names and ranges (Vital's source code,
`synth_parameters.cpp` and `synth_strings.h`; the Surge XT User Manual), played by this page's engine.

- **Vital:** three oscillators that read a **wavetable** (a row of waves; **Wave frame** picks one). Here every oscillator reads
  one table of this page's own, sine → triangle → square → saw, after Vital's *Basic Shapes* (name and order unverified). Envelope 2
  and LFO 1 can move the wave frame, as on the PPG Wave; the other synths have no wavetable, so a Vital patch reaches them as the
  nearest fixed wave. One filter (12 dB, 24 dB or notch; blend low · band · high), two envelopes, chorus, delay and reverb.
- **Surge XT:** two **Classic** oscillators (Shape: pulse · saw · dual saw; Width 1; Sub Mix on Osc 1), a mixer with ring
  modulation 1×2 and noise, Filter 1 (Vintage Ladder, 12 / 24 dB low-pass, band-pass, high-pass, notch), Filter EG, Amp EG, one LFO.
  The dual saw is played as one saw, and the real third oscillator is left out.
- What the beginner panel lacks is marked *cannot be done* in the report, with a reminder that the real plug-in may well have it.
- Beginner lessons, each ending with how to install the free plug-in and copy the patch across:
  [Meet Vital](intro-vital.qmd) and [Meet Surge XT](intro-surge-xt.qmd). The [Model D page](model-d.qmd)'s **As Vital** and
  **As Surge XT** views show one Model D patch in each plug-in's names.

## What if…

Some panels have a **What if…** menu: features the real instrument does not have, or fixes for things players miss, such as six
voices or a release stage on the Model D, a resonant filter on the DX7, a second oscillator on the Juno-60, an LFO on the Taurus
(which the Taurus III later added). Each says where the lack is documented, or that the wish is "commonly said, unverified". With
one on, the panel gets a **dashed orange outline** and the badge **What if — not the real instrument**. Only the sound changes:
the report still describes the real instrument, so its *the same / close / cannot* lines do not move, and a saved patch file lists
the what-ifs separately (`whatif`).

## Why they differ

The Model D manual calls it "a direct descendant of the Moog modular synthesizers". In place of patch cables it uses
colour-coded rocker switches: orange to connect modulation, blue to turn sounds on and off, white for performance features
and black to choose between sources (Model D manual p. 15). That made it fast to set up on stage, and it played one note.
Dave Smith, who designed the Prophet-5, writes that he "had the notion that these new-ish things called microprocessors
might be useful in designing … a fully programmable polyphonic synthesizer — the first of its kind" (Prophet-5 guide p. x).
The 1981 technical manual describes a Z-80 microprocessor scanning the keys, sharing them out among five voices and keeping 40
programs in memory.

This page's own reading, not from either manual, is that a microprocessor and five copies of a voice explain most of the
lists above. Two oscillators a voice rather than three kept five voices affordable, and Poly Mod put a modulating
oscillator, like the Model D's third, back inside every voice.

## History, players and records

Facts in this section are from Wikipedia's articles on each synth and the sources they cite (listed below).

### Minimoog Model D

- **Made:** introduced in 1970, designed by Bill Hemsath and other engineers with Robert Moog; prototypes A to C came first
  and the Model D in early 1970. Produced from 1970 to 1981, over 12,000 in 13 years. Reissued in 2016–17 and again in 2022.
- **Firsts:** the first synthesizer sold in ordinary retail shops, and the first with a pitch wheel.
- **Styles:** first popular in progressive rock and jazz, then disco, pop, rock, electronic music and funk.
- **Players and records:** Sun Ra's *My Brother the Wind* (1970), perhaps its first recording. Rick Wakeman used five on stage;
  Keith Emerson played one. Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea and Dick Hyman were early jazz users, and Stevie Wonder used it. The bass of
  Parliament's "Flash Light". Kraftwerk's *Autobahn* (1974) and *The Man-Machine* (1978). In disco, ABBA and Giorgio Moroder. In
  electronic music, Tangerine Dream, Klaus Schulze and Gary Numan.

### Prophet-5

- **Made:** designed by Dave Smith and John Bowen in 1977 and shown at the NAMM show in January 1978: the first polyphonic synth
  with fully programmable memory. Rev 1 (182 made), Rev 2, and Rev 3 (almost 6,000, on CEM chips), made from 1978 to 1984; Rev 4
  in 2020. It cost US$3,995 (Rev 1 and 2) and $4,595 (Rev 3).
- **Players and records:** Greg Hawkes of the Cars on "Let's Go" (1979) and "Shake It Up" (1981). Phil Collins, "In the Air
  Tonight" (1981). Japan, "Ghosts" (1982). Michael Jackson's *Thriller* (1982), Madonna's *Like a Virgin* (1984), Peter Gabriel's
  *So* (1986), Radiohead's *Kid A*, including "Everything In Its Right Place". Kraftwerk took it on their 1981 *Computer World* tour;
  Ryuichi Sakamoto used it on *Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence* and with Yellow Magic Orchestra.
- **Film:** Vangelis, *Blade Runner* (1982); Brad Fiedel, *The Terminator* (1984, on a Prophet-10); John Carpenter.

### TB-303

- **Made:** by Roland, designed by Tadao Kikumoto (who also designed the TR-909), released in 1981 at US$395 as a "computerised
  bass machine" to replace the bass guitar. A commercial failure, discontinued in 1984.
- **Styles:** cheap second-hand units became a foundation of acid house, Chicago house and techno.
- **Players and records:** Charanjit Singh, *Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat* (1982). Orange Juice, "Rip It Up" (1983), the
  first UK top-ten single with it. Phuture, "Acid Tracks" (1987). Hardfloor, "Acperience" (1992); Josh Wink, "Higher State of
  Consciousness" and Daft Punk, "Da Funk" (1995); Fatboy Slim, "Everybody Needs a 303" (1996).

### Juno-60

- **Made:** by Roland from 1982 to 1984, after the Juno-6 (May 1982, US$1,295); the Juno-60 (September 1982) added patch memory.
  Its digitally controlled oscillators stayed in tune; its chorus was meant to make up for the single oscillator.
- **Players and records:** a-ha, "Take On Me"; George Michael, "A Different Corner"; Cyndi Lauper, "Time After Time". Also
  Enya, Vince Clarke, Howard Jones, Eurythmics, Wham!, and Chicago house; later Metronomy.

### ARP 2600

- **Made:** by ARP Instruments from 1971 to 1981, designed by a team led by Alan R. Pearlman with Dennis Colin; US$2,600.
  Semi-modular, marketed to schools and universities. Korg reissued it in 2020 (2600 FS) and 2022 (2600 M).
- **Players and records:** Edgar Winter, Stevie Wonder (labelled in Braille), Pete Townshend, Joe Zawinul, Herbie Hancock. Tony
  Banks of Genesis from *A Trick of the Tail*. Black Sabbath, "Who Are You?" on *Sabbath Bloody Sabbath*. Ben Burtt made R2-D2's
  voice with it. Michael Jackson, "Thriller" (1983); Nine Inch Nails, "The Becoming".

### OB-Xa

- **Made:** by Oberheim, released December 1980 after the OB-X; 4, 6 or 8 voices, split and layer, 2-pole or 4-pole filtering,
  Curtis chips. Wikipedia's article names no players or records.

### MS-20

- **Made:** by Korg from 1978 to 1983: semi-modular, monophonic, high-pass and low-pass filters in series, a patch panel. Reissued
  as the MS-20 Mini (2013), kits (2014, 2015) and the MS-20 FS (2020). Wikipedia's article names no players or records.

### DX7

- **Made:** by Yamaha in 1983, on John Chowning's FM synthesis licensed from Stanford; presets by Dave Bristow and Gary
  Leuenberger. More than 200,000 sold, one of the best-selling synthesizers.
- **Players and records:** Ryuichi Sakamoto; Prince, "When Doves Cry"; Tina Turner, "The Best"; Sade, "Smooth Operator"; Michael
  Jackson, "Smooth Criminal". The "Bass 1" preset on a-ha's "Take On Me" and Kenny Loggins's "Danger Zone"; "Bass 2" on Berlin's
  "Take My Breath Away". "E Piano 1" on 40% of the US number-one singles of 1986. Brian Eno, *Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks*
  (1983).

### PPG Wave

- **Made:** by Palm Products GmbH (Wolfgang Palm), from 1981 to 1987: Wave 2, 2.2 and 2.3; US$7,000–10,000 at first.
- **Players:** a-ha, Alphaville, David Bowie, Depeche Mode, Rush, Tears for Fears, Talk Talk, Ultravox, Thomas Dolby, Stevie Wonder
  and many more (Wikipedia's list names no songs).

### Prophet-6

- **Made:** released by Sequential in 2015 (Wikipedia, "Sequential (company)"). Its manual describes it as a six-voice analog
  polysynth with touches "that the original never had, such as stereo outputs, velocity and aftertouch sensitivity, dual digital
  effects, a high-pass filter, a polyphonic step sequencer, an arpeggiator, and of course, MIDI" (Prophet-6 manual).

### Moog Taurus

- **Made:** designed by David Luce for Moog's unreleased Constellation; Taurus I 1975–1981, Taurus II 1981–1983 (the Moog Rogue's
  engine), Taurus III 2010–2012 (1,000 made).
- **Players and records:** Genesis, Yes, Rush, Pink Floyd, Tool, Dream Theater, U2, the Police; Phil Collins, "I Don't Care
  Anymore"; Harmonium on *Harmonium en tournée*.

### Minimoog Voyager

- **Made:** designed by Robert Moog, released by Moog Music in 2002 (US$2,995; the first 600, signed, $3,495) and discontinued in
  2015 after more than 14,000. The Old School version (2008–2009) had no touch pad and no MIDI. Wikipedia's article names no records.

### Moog Sub 37

- **Made:** by Moog Music from 2014, an analog signal path with digital modulators; the Subsequent 37 followed in 2017.
  Wikipedia's article names no players or records.

### Moog Grandmother

- **Made:** a semi-modular, 32-key two-oscillator monosynth by Moog Music, with circuits based on the Model 15 modular and the
  Minimoog; patches cannot be saved. Wikipedia's article names no players or records.

### Memorymoog

- **Made:** by Moog Music from 1982 to 1985, its last polyphonic synthesizer before the company's 1987 bankruptcy: six voices of
  three oscillators, often described as six Minimoogs in one. The Memorymoog Plus added MIDI.
- **Players and records:** Jan Hammer on *Miami Vice*; Geoff Downes on Asia's *Alpha* (1983); Jon Lord on *Before I Forget* and with
  Whitesnake and Deep Purple; Space Art, *Trip in the Centre Head*; Jim Gilmore of Saga; David Bryan of Bon Jovi.

## Build it from a video

Each video below rebuilds a famous record's sound on the real instrument. Watch it, press **Build …** for the song (that fills in
the form), set the panel the way the video does, listen, and press **Download the patch file**. Write in the notes what you had to
guess: a video shows the knobs, but this page's knobs are not the real ones (see [What is checked](#what-is-checked-and-what-is-not)).
Your teacher adds the files to the **Library** under the synths, marked *settings from the video (student)* until checked against
the record. Use **Open a patch file** to load one again.

## Reading the pictures

- **Signal flow** (inside each panel): oscillators and noise into the mixer, then the filter and the amplifier, with the
  modulation wires drawn and lit while they act. A wire or box drawn in **red** is a part of the starting patch that the
  other synth cannot copy.
- **Filter**: how loud each frequency comes out of each synth's filter with its current knobs, for middle C. The resonance
  peak and the 24 dB slope are drawn from the engine's own filter model, simplified to a straight-line (linear) version,
  so overload is not shown.
- **Envelopes**: both synths' filter envelopes (thin lines) and loudness envelopes (thick lines) for a key held one
  second. Flip the Prophet's **Rev** switch to see its envelope change from curved to almost straight, as the Prophet's
  guide describes.
- **Mixer drive**: what the mixer does to a signal as it gets louder. The line stays straight while the sound is clean,
  then flattens at the top once the mixer overloads.
- **Scope and spectrum**: the waves as they sound, and their harmonics.

## What is checked and what is not

Checked against the manuals: every control's name, the waves and ranges each oscillator has, the filter types and their
slope, envelope stages, LFO rates and shapes, which sources can modulate which targets, voices and unison, the pitch wheel
ranges, glide, the Model D's feedback path and its default low-note priority. Each line of the report names its page.

This page's own choices, not from the manuals: how the Prophet's 0 to 10 knobs map to hertz, seconds and octaves; the
curves between the Model D's printed end points; the exact widths of the Model D's "wide" and "narrow" pulses; the shape of
its triangle-sawtooth wave; modulation depths; unison detune in cents; and how the three filters differ (one model with
three settings, not simulations of the real circuits). Nobody has yet compared these sounds with the real instruments.

For the Prophet-6 and the Moog family the same holds: knob curves, the effect algorithms (delays, chorus, phasers, reverbs, the
distortion), the Voyager's second filter, the Duo-mode filter and every "What if…" are this page's own; the Sub 37 is cited from
the Subsequent 25 manual; the Taurus and Memorymoog manuals are OCR'd scans; and the five Moogs share one filter model, so how
their filters differ is not measured.

"Minimoog Voyager." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog_Voyager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimoog_Voyager). History section.

"Moog Grandmother." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Grandmother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Grandmother). History section.

"Moog Sub 37." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Sub_37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Sub_37). History section.

"Moog Taurus." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Taurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_Taurus). History section; the Taurus III added an LFO (the page's What if… on the Taurus).

"Oberheim OB-Xa." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_OB-Xa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_OB-Xa). History section.

"Sequential (company)." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequential_(company)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequential_(company)). The Prophet-6's release in 2015.

"Yamaha DX7." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_DX7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamaha_DX7). History section: FM licence, sales, presets and the records they are on.

**For students**

Korg. *ARP 2600 M Owner's Manual*. Korg Inc., 2021, [www.analoguehaven.com/korg/arp-2600-m/manual.pdf](https://www.analoguehaven.com/korg/arp-2600-m/manual.pdf). Block diagram and every normalled connection: VCOs (pp. 7-9), VCF (p. 10), ADSR and AR (p. 11), VCA (p. 12), mixer and reverb (p. 13), noise and voltage processors (p. 14), sample and hold (p. 15).

Korg. *MS-20 Owner's Manual*. Keio Electronic Laboratories, 1978, [www.korg.com/us/support/download/manual/0/131/2441/](https://www.korg.com/us/support/download/manual/0/131/2441/). VCOs, waveforms and ring modulator, high-pass and low-pass filters with peak up to self-oscillation (p. 5); EG 1, EG 2 with hold, MG, the patch panel (pp. 6-7). A scan, read by OCR.

Moog Music. *Minimoog Model D* [owner's manual, 2016 reissue]. Moog Music Inc., [cdn.inmusicbrands.com/Moog/Model%20D/Minimoog_Model_D_Manual.pdf](https://cdn.inmusicbrands.com/Moog/Model%20D/Minimoog_Model_D_Manual.pdf). Oscillators, waves and ranges (pp. 16-19), modulation (pp. 19-24), mixer and the external-input feedback (pp. 26-27, 33, 36), ladder filter, key tracking and contours (pp. 29-31), recipes (pp. 39-42), note priority (p. 47), specifications (p. 80); the patch sheets redrawn in "The Model D patch sheets" (pp. 55-76, 44 sounds; blank sheets pp. 77-79), read from the printed pages to the nearest half mark.

Oberheim. *OB-Xa Operation Manual*. Oberheim Electronics, [soundprogramming.net/manuals/Oberheim_OB-Xa_Manual.pdf](https://soundprogramming.net/manuals/Oberheim_OB-Xa_Manual.pdf). Unison and the low-note rule (p. 8); the LFO, 0.1-20 Hz, sine / square / S&H (p. 9); oscillators, sync and F-ENV to oscillator 2 (p. 10); 2-pole 12 dB and 4-pole 24 dB filter (p. 11); envelopes (p. 12); 8 voices, split and double (p. 13). A scan, read by OCR.

Roland. *Juno-60 Owner's Manual*. Roland Corporation, Apr. 1983, [soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_Juno-60_Manual.pdf](https://soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_Juno-60_Manual.pdf). Six voices and 56 patches (p. 2); DCO with no portamento, PWM, sub-oscillator, noise (pp. 12-13); HPF and VCF (p. 14); VCA and envelope (p. 16); LFO with delay (p. 17); chorus I and II (p. 22); specifications (p. 32). A scan, read by OCR.

Roland. *TB-303 Bass Line Owner's Manual*. Roland Corporation, Dec. 1981, [soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_TB-303_Manual.pdf](https://soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_TB-303_Manual.pdf). The tone control section: cutoff, resonance, env mod, decay, accent, waveform (p. 34); writing accent and slide (p. 40); specifications: two waveforms, pitch, length, accent and slide stored per step (p. 89). A scan, read by OCR.

Sequential. *Prophet-5 User's Guide*. Version 1.0, Sequential LLC, Oct. 2020, [vintageking.com/cdn/shop/files/sequential-prophet-5-manual.pdf](https://vintageking.com/cdn/shop/files/sequential-prophet-5-manual.pdf). Dave Smith's foreword (p. x), oscillators and sync (pp. 17-20), mixer (p. 21), the Rev 1/2 and Rev 3 filters and envelopes (pp. 22-30), LFO and wheel-mod (pp. 31-33), Poly Mod (pp. 34-35), vintage, wheels, glide, unison, chord memory, release, priority (pp. 36-45), recipes (pp. 46-52), used with the tutorials of pp. 8, 23, 26, 30 as starting patches (apps/shared/lessons/prophet-sheets.js).

Sequential. *Prophet-6 Operation Manual*. Version 1.0, Dave Smith Instruments, June 2015, [analoguehaven.com/sequential/prophet-6/manual.pdf](https://analoguehaven.com/sequential/prophet-6/manual.pdf). Printed page = PDF page - 10. Six voices; oscillators with continuously variable shape, sync, low freq (pp. 15-17); slop (p. 18); mixer and triangle sub octave (p. 19); 4-pole LP and 2-pole HP (pp. 20-23); envelopes (pp. 22-26); two effect slots and their types (pp. 26-28); LFO (pp. 31-33); Poly Mod (pp. 33-34); distortion (p. 41); unison (p. 43). Its recipes are the page's Prophet-6 examples.

Surge Synth Team. *Surge XT*. [surge-synthesizer.github.io/](https://surge-synthesizer.github.io/). Download page.

Surge Synth Team. "Surge XT User Manual." *Surge XT*. [surge-synthesizer.github.io/manual-xt/](https://surge-synthesizer.github.io/manual-xt/). Released as open source by Claes Johanson in September 2018; Classic oscillator (Shape, Width 1, Sub Mix); mixer with ring 1x2 / 2x3 and noise; filter types; FEG > F1, Keytrack > F1; Filter and Amp EG; LFO shapes and rate range; Play Mode; Bend Depth; installing.

Tytel, Matt. "README." *Vital*, GitHub repository mtytel/vital. [github.com/mtytel/vital#readme](https://github.com/mtytel/vital#readme). "A spectral warping wavetable synthesizer"; GPLv3 source; "the free version of Vital"; download at vital.audio after making an account.

Vital Audio. *Vital: Spectral Warping Wavetable Synth*. [vital.audio/](https://vital.audio/). Drag-and-drop modulation; the Basic tier (75 presets, 25 wavetables), Plus and Pro; Windows 10+, macOS 10.15+, Ubuntu 18.04+.

Yamaha. *DX7 Digital Programmable Algorithm Synthesizer Operation Manual*. Yamaha Corporation, [homepages.abdn.ac.uk/d.j.benson/pages/dx7/manuals/dx7-man.pdf](https://homepages.abdn.ac.uk/d.j.benson/pages/dx7/manuals/dx7-man.pdf). 16-note polyphony and 32 memories (introduction); operators, carriers and modulators (p. 23); 32 algorithms, carriers of algorithms 1, 5, 16 and 32 (p. 24); feedback (p. 25); envelopes (p. 26); the first FM exercise (pp. 34-35); glossary (p. 62).

**For teachers**

ARP Instruments. *ARP 2600 Owner's Manual*. ARP Instruments, Inc., 1971 (7th printing 1976), [www.korg.com/us/support/download/manual/0/842/4469/](https://www.korg.com/us/support/download/manual/0/842/4469/). The voltage-controlled filter falls off at 24 dB per octave (section 4.12). Chapter 5's patches (5.1-5.1401, PDF pp. 54-89) are the ARP 2600 starting patches in the Example menu, read from its text (the panel drawings are too small to read). A scan, read by OCR.

Jungleib, Stanley. *Prophet-5 Synthesizer Technical Manual*. 2nd ed., Sequential Circuits, Oct. 1981, [medias.audiofanzine.com/files/sequentialcircuitsprophet-5servicemanual-text-470674.pdf](https://medias.audiofanzine.com/files/sequentialcircuitsprophet-5servicemanual-text-470674.pdf). For Revisions 3.0-3.2: the Z-80 microcomputer reads the keyboard and knobs and assigns voices; 40 programs in NV RAM (section 2).

"Korg MS-20." *Wikipedia*, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korg_MS-20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korg_MS-20). 1978-1983, monophonic, semi-modular, high-pass and low-pass filters in series; the 2014 kit's two filter types.

Levien, Raph. "fm_core.cc." *Music Synthesizer for Android*, Google, Apache License 2.0, [github.com/google/music-synthesizer-for-android/blob/master/app/src/main/jni/fm_core.cc](https://github.com/google/music-synthesizer-for-android/blob/master/app/src/main/jni/fm_core.cc). The DX7's 32 algorithms as a table of operator buses, used by the page's engine; checked against the DX7 manual's carrier counts, not diagram by diagram.

Moog Music. *Grandmother User's Manual*. Moog Music Inc., 2018, [archive.org/details/MoogGrandmotherUsersManual](https://archive.org/details/MoogGrandmotherUsersManual). Cited by PDF page: overview (PDF 7), glide (PDF 10), oscillators and sync (PDF 11-12), mixer and the high-pass tip (PDF 14-15), filter (PDF 16-17), envelope (PDF 18-19), VCA modes and spring reverb (PDF 21), modulation (PDF 23).

Moog Music. *Memorymoog Owner's Manual* (Model 345). Moog Music Inc., [archive.org/details/synthmanual-moog-memorymoog-owners-manual](https://archive.org/details/synthmanual-moog-memorymoog-owners-manual). A scan, read by OCR; cited by PDF page: six voices of three oscillators, 100 programs (PDF 5), mono and glide (PDF 9), LFO (PDF 14), Voice Modulation (PDF 15), oscillators (PDF 16), mixer and filter (PDF 17).

Moog Music. *Minimoog Voyager Old School User's Manual*. Moog Music Inc., [archive.org/details/manualzilla-id-7334103](https://archive.org/details/manualzilla-id-7334103). Cited by PDF page: three variable-waveform oscillators (PDF 6), sync, linear FM, Dual LP and HP/LP filters with spacing (PDF 8), mod busses and LFO (PDF 9), external input overdrive (PDF 11-12).

Moog Music. *Subsequent 25 Owner's Manual*. Moog Music Inc., [www.adorama.com/col/productManuals/MGLPSSB00701.pdf](https://www.adorama.com/col/productManuals/MGLPSSB00701.pdf). Cited for the Sub 37 / Subsequent 37 features the family shares (their own manual could not be obtained): Duo Mode, ladder filter (PDF 9), waves (PDF 13), sync (PDF 14), sub oscillator (PDF 15), MultiDrive (PDF 16), the tutorial's cutoff 320 Hz and MultiDrive at 9 o'clock (PDF 19), LFO (PDF 20).

Moog Music. *Taurus Model 205A Owner's & Service Manual*. Moog Music Inc., [archive.org/details/moog_Moog_Taurus_Model_205A_Owners_Service_Manual](https://archive.org/details/moog_Moog_Taurus_Model_205A_Owners_Service_Manual). A scan, read by OCR; cited by PDF page. Two oscillators and BEAT, presets, octave, glide, filter contour, loudness (PDF 3-5); specifications: sawtooth, 24 dB VCF, glide 0-0.5 s (PDF 6).

"Oberheim Polyphonic Synthesizer." *Wikipedia*, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_SEM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberheim_SEM). The SEM's two-pole filter as low-pass, band-pass, high-pass or notch; two VCOs per voice.

PPG. *Wave 2.3 Service Manual*. Palm Products GmbH, [emusic-diy.org/_media/ppgmanuals:wave23.pdf](https://emusic-diy.org/_media/ppgmanuals:wave23.pdf). Eight voices, digital oscillators with wavetable EPROMs, SSM 2044 filters, panel pots reading 0-63 (PDF p. 5). No owner's manual was found. A scan, read by OCR.

"PPG Wave." *Wikipedia*, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPG_Wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPG_Wave). Years of the Wave 2, 2.2 and 2.3; two oscillators a voice on the 2.2 and 2.3; SSM 2044 24 dB filters.

Roland. *Juno-106 Owner's Manual*. Roland Corporation, [soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_Juno-106_Manual.pdf](https://soundprogramming.net/manuals/Roland_Juno-106_Manual.pdf). 128 patches, portamento and MIDI (p. 1); the HPF at 0 boosts the bass (p. 18); portamento (p. 23); chorus I and II not at the same time (p. 29). A scan, read by OCR.

"Roland Juno-60." *Wikipedia*, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Juno-60](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Juno-60). A 24 dB-per-octave resonant low-pass and a non-resonant high-pass filter; the chorus buttons' rates of 0.4 and 0.6 Hz.

"Roland TB-303." *Wikipedia*, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_TB-303](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_TB-303). Sawtooth or square; a 24 dB-per-octave resonant low-pass filter that does not self-oscillate; 1981-1984.

Sound On Sound. "PPG Wave 2.3 & Waveterm B" [review]. *Sound On Sound*, [www.soundonsound.com/reviews/ppg-wave-23-waveterm-b](https://www.soundonsound.com/reviews/ppg-wave-23-waveterm-b). 64 waves make a wavetable; 30 wavetables on the Wave 2.3.

Tytel, Matt. "synth_parameters.cpp." *Vital*, GitHub repository mtytel/vital. [github.com/mtytel/vital/blob/main/src/common/synth_parameters.cpp](https://github.com/mtytel/vital/blob/main/src/common/synth_parameters.cpp). Oscillator on, transpose, tune, level, wave frame, unison; filter cutoff 8-136 semitones, resonance, drive 0-20 dB, blend 0-2, key track; envelope times 0-2.378; LFO frequency -7..9; polyphony; portamento.

Tytel, Matt. "synth_strings.h." *Vital*, GitHub repository mtytel/vital. [github.com/mtytel/vital/blob/main/src/interface/look_and_feel/synth_strings.h](https://github.com/mtytel/vital/blob/main/src/interface/look_and_feel/synth_strings.h). Filter styles (12dB, 24dB, Notch Blend, Notch Spread, B/P/N) and models (Analog, Dirty, Ladder, Digital, Diode, Formant, Comb, Phaser).
